newsitem.title: UK: Amnesty questions fairness of Rwanda trials.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty questions fairness of Rwanda trials.

text.p: Amnesty International on Tuesday questioned the fairness of the first genocide trials in Rwanda, saying they prompted fears that many people would be unjustly executed.

The human rights organisation said the crimes committed during the genocide in 1994 shocked the world and devastated the lives of millions and it recognised the difficulty the government faced in conducting the trials.
"However, for the government's efforts and the trials themselves to be effective, they need to conform to international standards," the group said in a statement.
"Otherwise, justice will not be seen to be done and public confidence in the judiciary will not be restored," it added.

The first defendants, Deo Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former local administrator, were brought to trial on December 27 accused of organising massacres of Tutsis in Rwanda.
They are the first suspects to be tried under a genocide law.

Their trial lasted only four hours and Amnesty said the defendants had no access to legal counsel and were not given an opportunity of call their own witnesses or cross-examine prosecution witnesses. They were pronounced guilty a week later and sentenced to death.
There are about 90,000 Rwandans crammed into jails since being accused of taking part in the 1994 slaughter by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
Amnesty International called on Rwanda to ensure that the trials met international standards, including giving the defendants access to court files and adequate time to prepare their defence.
It also said the defendants should be assisted by legal counsel, including foreign lawyers, and be allowed to call and cross-examine witnesses.

"In a climate of bitterness and suspicion, there is a risk that those accused of genocide will be considered guilty unless proven innocent," the group said, adding that the use of the death penalty was a "form of official violence".
Amnesty also issued a report raising its concerns on the forcible repatriation of refugees from Tanzania, Zaire and Burundi and the risk that they may face further human rights violations in Rwanda.
